blocks.prompt: The Scorpion That Glows in the Dark
blocks.text: A scorpion is not an insect. Insects have six legs. A scorpion has eight. That makes it an arachnid, like a spider. In front, a scorpion has two claws called pincers. It uses them to grab a cricket and hold it still. Behind, it has a tail that curls over its back. At the tip is a stinger. Most scorpions hide under rocks and logs all day. They hunt at night, when the sand is cool. Here is the strangest part. If you shine a special blue light on a scorpion, its whole body glows green. Scientists still do not know why it does that.

blocks.prompt: The Hunter That Cannot See You
blocks.text: Count the legs on a scorpion and you get eight. That one fact tells you it is not an insect at all. It is an arachnid, a cousin of spiders, ticks, and mites. A scorpion is built like a tool. Two pincers reach out in front to grab and hold. The long tail arches over its back, and at the tip sits a stinger loaded with venom. A big scorpion with heavy pincers often has weak venom, because it can simply crush its meal. A small scorpion with thin pincers usually has strong venom instead. It cannot win a wrestling match, so it wins with chemistry. Scorpions have as many as twelve eyes, and they still see very poorly. They hunt by feeling instead. Tiny hairs and slits on their legs pick up the shiver of a beetle walking across the sand, and the scorpion turns and strikes without ever seeing it. Then there is the glow. Under ultraviolet light, a scorpion shines a bright blue-green, as if someone switched it on. The glow comes from a thin layer in its shell. Scientists have argued about it for years and still cannot agree on what it is for.

blocks.prompt: The Hunter That Feels the Ground
blocks.text: Scorpions are older than almost everything you can name. They were crawling around more than 430 million years ago, before the first tree, before the first dinosaur, before flowers existed. The earliest ones lived in water. Their shape has barely changed since. That shape works. In front are two pincers for grabbing. Behind is a segmented tail that arches over the back and ends in a stinger. Underneath, hidden against the belly, is a pair of comb-shaped organs called pectines that no other animal on Earth has. The scorpion drags them lightly over the ground, tasting it, reading who has passed by. A scorpion may have as many as twelve eyes and still be nearly blind. It does not need sight. Slits and fine hairs on its legs detect vibrations traveling through sand, and the scorpion works out the direction and distance of a beetle from the tiny gap in time between one leg feeling the tremor and another. Its venom is a mixture, not a single poison, and each species brews a different recipe. Of roughly two thousand species, only about twenty-five are dangerous to a person. The general rule is a trade: strong pincers, weak venom; weak pincers, strong venom. A mother scorpion does not lay eggs. She gives birth to live young, and they climb onto her back and ride there, pale and soft, until their first molt hardens them.

blocks.prompt: Four Hundred Million Years of Practice
blocks.text: A scorpion is a machine that stopped being improved a very long time ago, because it was already finished. Fossils of scorpions go back more than 430 million years, to a world with no trees, no flowers, no dinosaurs, and no animals at all on dry land. The first scorpions lived in shallow seas. Put one of those fossils beside a scorpion alive today and you would struggle to explain what evolution had been doing for the last four hundred million years. Pincers in front. Segmented tail curved over the back. Stinger at the tip. The design simply worked. It works because it solves the whole problem of eating. The pincers, properly called pedipalps, grab and hold. The stinger delivers venom, which is not one chemical but a cocktail of dozens, tuned by each species over millions of years. There is a rough trade running through the family: species with thick, powerful pincers tend to have mild venom, because they can crush what they catch, while species with slender pincers tend to carry potent venom, because chemistry is the only weapon they have. Of about two thousand species, only twenty-five or so are genuinely dangerous to humans. Sensing is where the scorpion becomes strange. It may carry up to twelve eyes and still be effectively blind. Instead it listens with its legs. Slit sensilla in the leg joints register vibrations rippling through sand, and the scorpion compares the arrival time at each of its eight legs, calculating direction the way you would locate a shout by which ear heard it first. Beneath its body hang the pectines, comb-like organs found in no other animal, which it sweeps across the ground to read chemical traces left by prey and by other scorpions. Then there is the fluorescence. Hold an ultraviolet lamp over a desert at night and scorpions blaze blue-green out of the darkness, lit from within. The glow comes from compounds in a thin, hard layer of the shell. Nobody has settled on why. Perhaps it helps the scorpion judge moonlight and decide whether to hunt. Perhaps it lures insects. Perhaps it is a leftover of the shell chemistry and does nothing at all. A famously effective animal that we can now find in complete darkness still keeps its best secret.

notes: Order Scorpiones: about 430 million years old

Chlorotoxin from the deathstalker marks tumor tissue

blocks.prompt: Four Hundred Million Years, and Still Glowing
blocks.text: Almost every animal you can think of is a newcomer compared to the scorpion. The oldest scorpion fossils are about 430 million years old, from a period when the land was bare rock and moss, when there were no trees, no insects in the air, no flowers, no dinosaurs, and no ancestor of yours anywhere outside the water. Those first scorpions were water animals. Their descendants walked out onto an empty continent and have been there ever since, through four mass extinctions, on every continent except Antarctica. Set a 430-million-year-old fossil next to a scorpion from an Arizona backyard tonight and the resemblance is almost insulting: same pincers, same segmented tail carried in the same curve, same stinger. Evolution kept editing nearly everything else and left this animal alone. The reason is that the body plan answers the whole question of survival at once. The pincers, properly the pedipalps, grab and pin. The tail, called the metasoma, is not a tail in the way a lizard's is; it is the back end of the abdomen, and it swings the stinger forward over the head with speed that is hard to see. The venom inside is not a single substance but a blend of dozens of small proteins, each one shaped to jam a particular kind of nerve channel. Different species mix different blends. Across roughly two thousand species, only about twenty-five carry venom that seriously threatens a human, and there is a rough rule behind that: heavy-pincered species tend to have weak venom because they can simply overpower their prey, while slender-pincered species tend to have the potent stuff because chemistry is all they have. That chemistry has turned out to be worth studying. One protein from the deathstalker scorpion, chlorotoxin, binds tightly to certain tumor cells and not to healthy tissue. Researchers attached a fluorescent dye to it, and in surgical trials the edge of a tumor has glowed while surgeons worked. An animal built to end small lives is helping to save large ones. Its senses are stranger than its weapons. A scorpion may carry as many as twelve eyes and remain, for practical purposes, blind. It hunts by touch instead. Slits in the joints of its legs, called slit sensilla, register vibrations moving through sand, and because the eight legs are spread apart, each one feels the tremor at a slightly different instant. The scorpion reads those tiny delays and turns straight toward the source, the same trick your brain performs when it tells you which side of a room a sound came from. Under the belly hang the pectines, comb-shaped organs that exist in no other animal alive, dragged across the ground to taste it and learn what has walked there. It is also patient in a way that borders on the ridiculous. A scorpion can slow its metabolism to a fraction of normal and survive a year on a single insect. A mother does not lay eggs. She gives birth to living young, and they climb onto her back and ride there, soft and white, until their first molt hardens their shells. And then there is the glow. Sweep an ultraviolet lamp across a desert at night and scorpions light up blue-green, unmistakable, dozens of them where a moment ago there was only sand. The fluorescence comes from compounds locked into the hyaline layer of the shell, and after decades of argument nobody can say what it is for. Perhaps it lets the scorpion measure moonlight and decide whether to hunt. Perhaps it draws insects closer. Perhaps it is simply a by-product of hardening the shell, meaning nothing. The oldest, most tested design in the animal kingdom, and we can find every one of them in the dark without knowing why they answer.
